title: Zero-Knowledge Predicate Proofs Between AI Agents: A Measured, Cross-Protocol Gateway and the Source-Integrity Gap
abstract: Multi-agent AI platforms move quickly from staging to production, but the way agents establish trust remains rudimentary: an agent either transmits raw data to a peer or accepts that peer's natural-language self-report that a value complies with policy. The first over-shares; the second is unverifiable and is exactly the channel prompt injection attacks. Prevailing responses emphasise identity, visibility, and post-hoc detection, and recent proposals for cryptographically enforced agent policy have been evaluated in simulation rather than execution. We take provable data minimisation between agents from proposal to running system. In our Zero-Knowledge Proof Gateway, agents exchange proofs of governance-defined predicates over private data rather than the data itself, so exposure is prevented by design rather than detected afterwards; because no interoperability protocol can carry such a proof, we propose a slot and implement it on both MCP and Agent2Agent from one endpoint. A 32-bit threshold predicate proves in 6.2 ms and verifies in 1.0 ms with a 608-byte Bulletproofs proof on one commodity vCPU; eleven adversarial experiments and nineteen protocol checks pass; and the system is deployed to Kubernetes with empirically verified network isolation. Our case study proves a retail client order is within its limit without revealing the amount, instantiating the GDPR data-minimisation principle as an enforced technical measure of the kind EU law now names explicitly. We then address the limitation no comparable work resolves: a predicate proof binds a statement to a committed value, never to the system of record. We give a construction fusing an enclave attestation with the proof in both directions, so verifying one artifact certifies jointly that the predicate holds and that the value was read by a specific measured binary, and test it against a mock authority.

title: Secure and trustworthy energy systems: A four-layer threat model and defense-in-depth framework
Reproducibility is the New Copyleft: Defining AGI-oriented Reproducible Builds
abstract: Copyleft, as implemented in licenses such as the GNU General Public License, was a legal hack that used copyright to guarantee user freedom by tying the availability of source code to every act of distribution. Its normative force rested on an implicit technical premise: that source code and object code stand in a well-defined, humanly auditable, and reproducible relationship. Large language models and, prospectively, Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) systems systematically violate this premise. The artifacts jointly required to reconstruct a model -- code, data, weights, hyperparameters, toolchain, and hardware configuration -- are each subject to independent legal, technical, and economic constraints that no current open-source framework fully resolves. Sufficiently capable AI systems can also rewrite licensed source into functionally equivalent derivatives stripped of their original obligations, a form of laundering against which copyleft has no effective defense. This paper argues that a functional analogue of copyleft for AGI must be grounded not in share-alike clauses over code, but in reproducible builds: a practice guaranteeing bit-exact reconstructability from declared inputs. We review the logic of copyleft, critically examine Maffulli's Second Liberation thesis according to which AI fulfills Stallman's dream, and show that the argument collapses unless AGI systems are themselves reproducible. Drawing on the Open Source AI Definition (OSAID), the Model Openness Framework (MOF), OpenMDW, and deterministic-inference research, we define seven requirements for AGI-oriented reproducible builds. We further argue that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and analogous AI-to-AI coupling mechanisms constitute a new dynamic linking layer for which copyleft-style licensing is ill-suited, and that Masnick's "protocols, not platforms" framework offers a more promising governance template.

title: GenEvolve: Self-Evolving Image Generation Agents via Tool-Orchestrated Visual Experience Distillation
abstract: Open-ended image generation is no longer a simple prompt-to-image problem. High-quality generation often requires an agent to combine a model's internal generative ability with external resources. As requests become more diverse and demanding, we aim to develop a general image-generation agent that can self-evolve through trajectories and use tools more effectively across varied generation challenges. To this end, we propose GenEvolve, a self-evolving framework based on Tool-Orchestrated Visual Experience Distillation. In GenEvolve, each generation attempt is modeled as a tool-orchestrated trajectory, where the agent gathers evidence, selects references, invokes generation skills, and composes them into a prompt-reference program. Unlike existing agentic generation methods that mainly rely on image-level scalar rewards, GenEvolve compares multiple trajectories for the same request and abstracts best-worst differences into structured visual experience, provided only to a privileged teacher branch. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation, Visual Experience Distillation provides dense token-level supervision, helping the student internalize better search, knowledge activation, reference selection, and prompt construction. We further construct GenEvolve-Data and GenEvolve-Bench. Experiments on public benchmarks and GenEvolve-Bench show substantial gains over strong baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance among current image-generation frameworks. Our website is as follows: https://ephemeral182.github.io/GenEvolve/

title: Towards an Understanding of Default Policies in Multitask Policy Optimization
abstract: Much of the recent success of deep reinforcement learning has been driven by regularized policy optimization (RPO) algorithms with strong performance across multiple domains. In this family of methods, agents are trained to maximize cumulative reward while penalizing deviation in behavior from some reference, or default policy. In addition to empirical success, there is a strong theoretical foundation for understanding RPO methods applied to single tasks, with connections to natural gradient, trust region, and variational approaches. However, there is limited formal understanding of desirable properties for default policies in the multitask setting, an increasingly important domain as the field shifts towards training more generally capable agents. Here, we take a first step towards filling this gap by formally linking the quality of the default policy to its effect on optimization. Using these results, we then derive a principled RPO algorithm for multitask learning with strong performance guarantees.

title: Self-Healing Mechanisms for Autonomous Cybersecurity Systems Using Reinforcement Learning
abstract: The increasing sophistication of cyber threats has driven the need for intelligent, adaptive cybersecurity systems capable of autonomous operation. Conventional security approaches, such as signature-based and rule-based detection mechanisms, often struggle to identify and respond effectively to evolving and previously unseen attack patterns. This study presents a reinforcement learning (RL)-based self-healing framework that enhances autonomous cybersecurity by improving threat detection, accelerating response and recovery, and increasing overall system resilience. The proposed framework employs reinforcement learning agents that continuously interact with the operating environment to learn and optimize defense strategies. Through ongoing adaptation, the system effectively detects emerging threats and autonomously initiates appropriate mitigation and recovery actions. Comparative performance analysis demonstrates that the RL-based framework consistently outperforms traditional security approaches across multiple cybersecurity metrics. Specifically, the proposed model achieves a threat detection accuracy of approximately 93%, exceeding the performance of conventional signature-based and anomaly-based methods, thereby demonstrating superior adaptability to previously unseen attacks. The framework also significantly reduces post-attack recovery time, achieving system restoration in approximately 30 seconds compared with substantially longer recovery periods required by manual and rule-based approaches. This rapid self-healing capability minimizes service disruption, limits the propagation of attacks, and enhances operational continuity, particularly in critical infrastructure environments. Furthermore, experimental evaluation indicates notable improvements in system resilience, including higher uptime, more effective threat mitigation, and improved response efficiency. By continuously refining its defensive policies through reinforcement learning, the proposed framework provides a robust, adaptive, and resilient cybersecurity solution capable of addressing the challenges posed by dynamic and sophisticated cyber threats.

title: ‘Would they be proud of us?’
abstract: In 1976, C. Langton Hewer, the first editor of this journal, wrote: ‘One of the advantages of resigning from the post of editor is that one need no longer write editorials’ [1]. The reason used by the then editor to persuade him to write another one was the 25th anniversary of the publication of Anaesthesia. Professor Harmer used the first issue of the millennium as his excuse and I agreed provided that I would not have to do it again when the millennium actually arrives. We have been fortunate in this country in that anaesthesia has been a physician-only specialty. The early pioneers were little more than ‘rag and bottle men’, although attempts were made to deliver accurately known concentrations of the two agents initially in use, ether and chloroform. A variety of apparatus was designed in attempts to achieve this latter aim, which would undoubtedly terrify the modern young anaesthetist. What would those pioneers think of us today? Would they believe what has happened to their speciality in the last 75 or so years and would they be proud of what they saw and what we have achieved? The essential component of our work in the operating theatre is the anaesthetic machine. This was designed in the early part of the last century by Boyle, a person who did not achieve the acclaim he deserved and who sadly died in relative poverty (D. J. Wilkinson, personal communication). There have been many changes made to this machine over the years, but the principle remains the same (although modern jargon calls it a workstation, it is still a machine). Pin index systems were added to prevent connection of the wrong cylinder, but accidents still happened. Even after introduction of piped gases, fatal accidents occurred and devices to detect failure of the oxygen supply are now an integral part of the machine. Monitoring of the inspired oxygen concentration is now regarded as essential and such a monitor is an integral part of the pre-use anaesthetic machine check. The development of potent volatile agents demanded use of accurately known concentrations and vaporisers were designed capable of meeting these demands over a wide range of fresh gas flows and temperatures. Systems are now available that allow vaporisers to be changed quickly on machines, allowing the anaesthetist the luxury of choosing a different agent without having to change the machine. But these systems have brought their own problems, particularly as the result of failure to check for leaks after the vaporiser has been changed. Such is the concern engendered by these systems that it was the subject of a recent editorial in this journal [2]. Failure to check the anaesthetic machine before use remains a constant problem and colleagues should be reminded that this is the job of the anaesthetist and no one else. It was only a relatively short time ago, within the author's anaesthetic life-time, that after checking the machine, connections had to be found that actually matched before proceeding. Out of this developed British, European and International Standards, probably the most boring committees that anyone could attend, but we must be forever grateful that there are people who are prepared to do this work; the effect on patient safety has been considerable. Techniques used in anaesthesia are usually demanded by surgical procedures. Thus maxillofacial surgery was responsible for one of the most significant advances of all, namely tracheal intubation, forever linked with the name of Magill, though others also played a significant part. This was originally performed blindly via the nose, but anaesthetists soon demanded that the larynx be seen for the passage of the tracheal tube and hence laryngoscopes were developed. These were modified for use in difficult cases and eventually led to the development of fibreoptic methods. There have been many other instances where anaesthetic techniques were designed or modified to meet surgical demands, e.g. hypothermia, controlled hypotension, wake-up tests during spinal surgery; cardiopulmonary bypass made many demands on the skills of the anaesthetists. Monitoring is now routine, with equipment which wasn't available 25 years or so ago. Gone are the days when if a trainee told a consultant that the patient's arterial blood pressure was 60 mmHg, he/she received the answer: ‘Then serve you right for taking it’ or ‘You can't have the ECG, the professor is using it’. End-tidal carbon dioxide measurement allows for accurate and adequate ventilation, while the concentration of volatile agents can also be monitored. We can now measure a large number of physiological variables and direct invasive cardiovascular measurements are routine during major surgery. All this information undoubtedly improves patient safety and allows us to achieve a patient in optimum condition after prolonged surgery. We must be grateful to the equipment manufacturers whose efforts on our behalf allow us to be able to do this. Still eluding us, however, are simple, practical methods of measuring blood flow and cardiac output, but they will come. Nevertheless, it is incumbent on any anaesthetist using this equipment to understand the mechanisms by which they work, otherwise monitoring itself can be potentially dangerous [3]. The drugs we use nowadays would be unrecognisable to those who practised in the first 50 years of the last century. They have become more potent, cleaner, shorter acting and controllable. We are no longer in danger of being blown-up by inhalational agents. Metabolism to toxic compounds has been virtually eliminated and even concerns regarding the degradation of sevoflurane have largely been unfounded. Intravenous induction of anaesthesia is virtually routine and from the 1930s to the 1990s, thiopental reigned supreme, despite many attempts to find a safer alternative. The only drug to challenge it and may now even replace it is propofol. Improvement in measurement techniques has allowed the quantification of very small amounts of drugs in body fluids and the discipline of pharmacokinetics emerged. It is possible to predict the performance of a drug and to design dosage regimens to attain therapeutic levels. This, together with the arrival of propofol and short-acting opioids, resulted in the development of total intravenous anaesthesia. At the same time, infusion pumps with the possibility of computer control were developed and which could also deliver accurate volumes over a very wide time-scale. A large number of opioids have appeared, but they are pharmacodynamically identical, differing only in their pharmacokinetic properties. Their use is unfortunately associated with a high incidence of nausea and vomiting, which remains one of the great challenges of anaesthetic practice. Regional anaesthetic techniques, especially epidural anaesthesia, only became extensively practised after the introduction of lidocaine in 1948. The search for a really long-acting local anaesthetic drug, however, has so far failed. We owe a large debt of gratitude to the pharmaceutical companies who have produced such excellent drugs for us over the years. It is therefore sad and disturbing to learn that some of the major companies have pulled out of ‘anaesthesia’. Are we really at the end of anaesthetic drugs as we know them? But the drug with the most profound effect since the discovery of anaesthesia itself has been curare. Introduced in the 1940s, it revolutionised anaesthetic and surgical practice. It was now possible to operate on anyone, however sick, as it allowed the performance of major and prolonged surgery at light planes of anaesthesia, thereby avoiding the profound depressant effects of high doses of volatile agents. Balanced anaesthesia remains the basis of general anaesthetic practice today. Nevertheless, two major problems were created by neuromuscular blocking drugs, namely the ‘can't intubate, can't ventilate’ scenario and awareness due to too light anaesthesia. Gradually, these problems are being solved, but a simple, practical monitor to eradicate the awareness problem has still not been found. Because of the use of curare, anaesthetists had to learn not only how to ventilate the lungs, but also about the physiology of artificial ventilation in those with normal and abnormal lungs. Being an ingenious bunch, anaesthetists developed machines to perform this task, thereby freeing their hands for other tasks. Development of these machines was gradually taken over by the equipment manufacturers and many such devices are available today. It was soon suggested that if we could ventilate the lungs of patients for several hours in the operating theatre, why couldn't we extend it for a few hours more postoperatively in specially designed areas. Hence intensive care was borne, all from the skills that anaesthetists had to develop following the use of one drug. Anaesthesia has also developed on the ‘political’ front. The London Society of Anaesthetists was founded in 1893 and became the anaesthetic section of the Royal Society of Medicine in 1908; the Association of Anaesthetists was founded in 1932. It is often forgotten that Magill played a large part in the formation of the Association and in the development of the DA examination, the first in anaesthesia. Pressure from the Association also led to the formation of the Faculty of Anaesthetists of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1948 and to the setting up of the Fellowship examination. Also, 1948 saw the inception of the National Health Service, which was an especially important time for anaesthesia as we were now recognised as a full specialty on an equal footing with all others. This took a long time to sink in with a lot of our colleagues in other disciplines, and it still seems to elude some even now! We are now the largest single hospital specialty and involved in many areas of hospital activity. The recent Audit Commission report ‘Anaesthesia under Examination’ revealed that an anaesthetic department underpins some 66% of the income of a hospital, yet their pay costs are equivalent to about 3% of contract income. As anaethetists we seem to be getting increasingly involved in management activities; there are some who no doubt enjoy such work, but the majority of anaesthetists would prefer to do the work that they were trained to do and want to do. Perhaps colleagues would be interested to know that the European Time Directive does not classify sitting on committees as work! There must obviously be some involvement in management issues, but it should not be allowed to take over; managers should be reminded from time to time of the words of Aneurin Bevan, the first Minister of Health: ‘It is doctors, dentists and nurses and their colleagues in the other health professions who provide the care and cure of patients and promote the health of people. It is the purpose of management to support them in giving that service’. With the passage of time it became obvious that we had outgrown our position in the Royal College of Surgeons. We owe an enormous amount to the surgeons and must never forget what they did for us in helping a developing specialty and they put no obstacles in our way when a separate College of Anaesthetists was formed. Since 1992, we have had the privilege of being a Royal College. The high standard of training in anaesthesia in the UK today is second to none in the world and due to the tireless efforts of our College. The 1960s and 70s in particular saw the rapid development of academic anaesthesia in the UK. Teaching programmes became available in every region and there was an explosion of anaesthetic research. It is from this research that the basis of our clinical practice is developed. Now universities are trying to close some of these departments and the ‘clinical academics’, to whom anaesthesia owes so much, are an endangered species. Universities are only interested in departments which can generate vast amounts of money from the grant-giving bodies, who in turn only seem to be interested in molecular biology; this is a very short-sighted policy. Perhaps they should remind themselves that the molecules are joined up to form cells, which in turn are joined up to form an entire organism, and who they themselves would liked to be looked after by when undergoing surgery, an anaesthetist trained in whole body physiology and pharmacology, or a molecular biologist. There are many more things that could have been mentioned, including our involvement in audit, but this editorial is already too long. Would those anaesthetists of long ago been proud of what we do and what we have achieved? As our American colleagues would say: ‘Damned right they would’. But would they actually recognise us? In 1918, Moore commented about anaesthetists: ‘The anaesthetist is a man apart . . . The ease and perfection of the operation largely depends upon his skill in giving the anaesthetic . . . The anaesthetist becomes a sort of prologue to the operation, his influence pervading the whole action, having an important but silent part in it and in the end, vanishing strangely’ [4]. They would indeed be impressed by what we do in the operating theatre, but they would find it difficult indeed to envisage our work in other areas such as obstetric units, pain clinics, palliative care, acute pain teams, intensive care, resuscitation and disaster medicine; even pre-operative visits were not a routine part of their practice. They would undoubtedly, however, agree, as the author does, with the words of Tom Boulton: ‘The foundation of our practice and professional expertise is the care of patients in the operating theatre’ [5].

title: Search and rescue system of systems modeling and virtual simulation
abstract: Search and Rescue (SAR) is one of the key supports for ensuring combat effectiveness, so it is of great significance to successfully conduct SAR actions to improve the operation capability. Due to the characteristics of complexity and multi-level combination of SAR, the analysis and design should pay attention to the following aspects: first, the high precision of a single capability indicator of the equipment platform is no longer the highest requirement, but the collaborative emergence of the comprehensive capability shown by the whole System of Systems (SoS) is more critical. Second, the personnel SAR in threatening environments is a large-scale, complex operation task, multi-equipment coordination required and multi-level joint SoS. Therefore, we need to take capability as a traction based on perspective of system engineering and carry out the structure modeling of personnel SAR SoS through the unified structure framework. Third, the personnel SAR SoS owns uncertainty and hierarchical emergence. Which modeling and simulation method should be selected to model and analyze the SoS from multiple perspectives, and how to combine simulation and Virtual Reality (VR) technology to play a role in assisting decision-making, so as to effectively improve the SAR capability. Therefore, this paper mainly carried out the following researches: (1) proposed the SoS design method based on EMCE (Environment, Mission, Capability and Elements) loop, and designed the personnel SAR SoS from four aspects: environment analysis, mission analysis, capability space planning and SoS elements analysis; (2) Based on DoDAF (Department of Defense Architecture Framework), the architecture of personnel SAR SoS was modeled, and the operational concept, operational nodes and information exchange, operational activities, state transition and event timing of the SAR SoS were designed in detail. (3) In view of the hierarchical emergence and simulation runtime of the SAR SoS, a composite modeling method adapted to the SAR SoS was proposed by taking advantage of the functional complementarity of the multi-Agent modeling method and DEVS (discrete event system) modeling method. (4) Using the holographic demonstration function of MR (mixed reality) equipment and the advantages of allowing users to interact with virtual objects and real objects, so as to assist commanders to better understand the virtual and real battlefield environment and make corresponding decisions.

title: Can Intellectual Property Law Regulate Behavior? A "Modest Proposal" for Weakening Unclean Hands
abstract: Surprisingly, current intellectual property law protects materials that are criminally prohibited or were made as a result of illegal criminal actions. Thus, a filmmaker may commit or induce various illegal acts, record them, and receive and enforce a copyright on the depictions, just as a corporation may patent drugs developed with stolen materials or through illegal experiments on human subjects. That creators who produce works with unclean hands may enjoy the benefits of federally protected monopolies is an oddity that requires scrutiny. This paper argues that a potential remedy to this situation would be the use of compliance conditions for copyright registration and patent grants. Though compliance conditions could be crafted in various ways, this paper suggests adopting federal legislation that would invalidate a copyright registration or a patent if the creator (or her agent) violated specific criminal laws in the immediate production of the material for which the protection is sought. Once implemented, compliance conditions might stop intellectual property laws from contributing, even remotely, to illegal conduct. This proposal also raises the more general question of when it is desirable to use one governmental function to aid the legitimate purposes of another. Thus, the viability of a compliance standard has potential implications for how we think about the disbursement of government privileges more broadly. The paper begins by examining how certain intellectual property doctrines already manifest some concern for compliance with various public policies. It then assesses the constitutionality of compliance conditions in intellectual property law and concludes by discussing the mechanics of implementing and administering a compliance standard in the more difficult context of copyright law. The paper ends with a suggestion of how a compliance standard can be justified.

title: AgentEHR: Advancing Autonomous Clinical Decision-Making via Retrospective Summarization
abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated profound utility in the medical domain.However, their application to autonomous Electronic Health Records (EHRs) navigation remains constrained by a reliance on curated inputs and simplified retrieval tasks.To bridge the gap between idealized experimental settings and realistic clinical environments, we present AGENTEHR.This benchmark challenges agents to execute complex clinical reasoning tasks, such as diagnosis and treatment planning, requiring long-range interactive reasoning directly within raw and high-noise databases.In tackling these tasks, we identify that existing summarization methods inevitably suffer from critical information loss and fractured reasoning continuity.To address this, we propose RETROSUM, a novel framework that unifies a retrospective summarization mechanism with an evolving experience strategy.By dynamically re-evaluating interaction history, the retrospective mechanism prevents long-context information loss and ensures unbroken logical coherence.Additionally, the evolving strategy bridges the domain gap by retrieving accumulated experience from a memory bank.Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that RETROSUM achieves performance gains of up to 29.16% over competitive baselines, while significantly decreasing total interaction errors by up to 92.3%.Our code and datasets are available at https: //github.com/BlueZeros/AgentEHR.
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)

title: AI-Driven Product Development: Cognitive Software Delivery at Enterprise Scale
abstract: Enterprise software development faces a significant challenge in harnessing the full potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools, which often operate as disconnected point solutions across the software delivery lifecycle. This fragmentation leads to context loss, redundant workflows, and missed opportunities for true digital transformation. This article introduces Cognitive Software Delivery (CSD), a framework designed to integrate isolated AI tools into a unified, context-aware ecosystem. CSD is built upon four foundational architectural components: the Enterprise Context Mesh (ECM) for unified, versioned knowledge management; the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for standardized and secure data access; Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for producing contextually grounded AI outputs; and Agent-to-Agent Orchestration (A2A) for intelligent, automated workflow coordination. Through seamless integration across market research, requirements engineering, design, development, testing, deployment, and continuous improvement, CSD addresses the interoperability and traceability gaps that hinder enterprise-scale AI adoption. Validation through multi-industry case studies demonstrates measurable benefits, including reductions in cycle time (up to two-thirds), defect rates (up to 90%), and review delays, alongside qualitative gains in developer satisfaction and organizational adaptability. While challenges remain—including infrastructure readiness, change management complexity, and ethical considerations such as AI bias and transparency—CSD’s modular architecture and continuous learning capabilities offer a practical and strategic pathway to accelerated, AI-native software engineering.
venue: Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies

title: The social production of the food environment: a mixed-methods analysis of the unequal distribution of capitals and competencies in a Latin American metropolis
abstract: Introduction: Food-environment models often privilege structural determinants and under-specify how eating practices and agency participate in (re)producing environments. This study analyzes, through a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, how social eating practices are shaped by food environments and, in turn, contribute to their differential configuration across two districts of contrasting socioeconomic status. It proposes a theoretical framework that articulates Bourdieu's praxeology with Shove's theory of practices, conceptualizing food environments as social fields in which capitals are contested, and meanings, materials, and competencies are stabilized. Methods: Through a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the NEMS-P-Ch survey was administered to 785 adults, and eleven focus groups were conducted in two districts of contrasting socioeconomic status (SES) within a major Latin American metropolis. Results: In low-SES districts, provisioning practices center on farmers' markets and local shops, mobilizing social capital and budget-maximizing strategies to navigate material scarcity. Conversely, high-SES practices are dominated by supermarkets and digital platforms, guided by time efficiency and taste as markers of distinction. Discussion: The food environment is both a producer and a product of daily practices, which configure differentiated infrastructures based on the agents' trajectories and available capitals. Public policies must move beyond isolated individual and structural approaches, integrating the complexity of social practices to effectively address the persistent structural inequalities of urban food systems.

title: The Composed Platform: one pre-deployment screen predicts a multi-capability frozen-token stack under cross-domain stress — with an axis-specific reach, on commodity silicon
abstract: The Composed Platform: one pre-deployment screen predicts a multi-capability frozen-token stack under cross-domain stress — with an axis-specific reach, on commodity silicon Randolph James Ferlic, M.D. and Kimberly Kate Ferlic — Fieldstone Analytics, LLC, Austin, TX, USA Preprint · Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23401467 · CC-BY 4.0 · Community: spiral-domain-encoder-campaign · a characterization of previously filed and published methods; no new algorithmic subject matter is disclosed. Abstract A frozen, deterministic single-token encoder exposes nine composable capabilities — accuracy, robustness, and monitoring — on one runtime, and a prior program has shown that a single class-separability measurement, computed once on a deployment's commissioning data, predicts the encoder's single-capability behavior across domains. This paper answers the question a technical evaluator actually asks: does the composed stack hold under cross-domain stress, and can one cheap probe de-risk the whole platform at once? We run a pre-registered study across sixteen domains spanning seven modality families and four stressors, with five falsifiable hypotheses and frozen bands. The central finding is an honest boundary, not a blanket win. Composition is free and deterministic. Across ninety-six capability-additions under stress, 100% are non-destructive (0 destructive beyond a max(0.01, seed-spread) margin), and the composed stack is bit-exact — 0 token flips on the host, anchored to 0/256 flips on two microcontroller architectures (float32 and int8). One screen predicts the composed safety gate — and its reach is axis-specific. A single commissioning-time separability measurement predicts the composed safety gate (Spearman +0.92, permutation p = 0.0002, thirteen domains), and that reach is axis-specific: the same screen is blind to corruption-robustness (Spearman −0.23, p = 0.39 — refuted exactly as pre-registered). The screen answers the accuracy, label-budget, and safety-gate questions, because those are properties of where the classes sit; it does not answer the corruption-robustness question, which is a property of how the input is degraded and needs its own input-conditioning dial. The honest mitigation limit. Label-free recentering recovers only ~30% of cross-domain loss (not a majority), so the deployment consequence is a requirement, not a defect: under drift the stack must be recalibrated per-epoch, and label-free recentering is a partial mitigation between recalibrations. It runs on commodity silicon, measured and hardened. On an Arm Cortex-M33 the frozen runtime is bit-exact (0/256 flips across two architectures, two models, and both numeric paths, replicated across twelve power-on resets); its worst-case inference latency is 1.573 ms with near-zero jitter (a spike, not a spread, 3× inside a 5 ms budget); a continuous 50,678-inference soak produced zero token changes and zero faults; per-inference energy is 9.73 ± 0.07 µJ on a sub-milliwatt idle floor; and on-device compute costs less than a single BLE advertising event (16.6 µJ, including the CPU wake and three-channel transmission), so shipping the one-byte token instead of the raw window saves roughly 20–70× in radio energy. Highlights · A composable platform, not features that fight each other: 96/96 capability-additions non-destructive under cross-domain stress; 0 token flips (0/256 on silicon). · One cheap commissioning probe predicts the composed safety gate (Spearman +0.92, p = 0.0002) — the program's separability law survives composition. · The honest boundary that makes the probe deployable: the same screen is blind to corruption-robustness (Spearman −0.23). Run the probe for the class-geometry axes; condition the input for the rest. · A stated requirement, not a hidden weakness: label-free recentering recovers only ~30% of cross-domain loss → recalibrate per-epoch under drift. · A measured, hardened silicon envelope: WCET 1.573 ms (≈0 jitter), a 50,678-inference zero-drift soak, 9.73 ± 0.07 µJ/inference, compute cheaper than one radio packet, 12.7 KB footprint, sub-milliwatt. · The economics of one byte (the deployment implications): on-device compute moves the energy bottleneck off the radio — ~25× lower energy per delivered decision and ~150–4,000× smaller transmit/store footprint, on a ~$10-class commodity microcontroller, with the raw waveform never leaving the device. · One platform, nine composable capabilities, five invariants: a deployment composes a subset on one runtime; Tier-0 on-device execution is the fifth architectural invariant (proven on silicon), and AI-safety runtime monitoring is the flagship application of the self-twin capability — not separate capabilities. · Two of five pre-registered hypotheses refuted — each refutation sharpening the claim rather than undermining it. What this record contains · Manuscript_Paper62.pdf / .docx — the manuscript (7 figures, 30 references). · PAPER_62_ZENODO_ARCHIVE.zip — the reproducibility archive: the frozen pre-registration (five hypotheses with a-priori bands), the composition-under-stress runner, the shared dataset loaders + the frozen token encoder + the composed-stack battery, the per-domain result records (JSON) and aggregate verdicts, the seven figures and their builder, and a README. Public corpora are not redistributed; absolute paths, handles, and productization know-how are scrubbed. Cite as Ferlic, R. J., & Ferlic, K. K. (2026). This work characterizes previously filed and published methods and discloses no new algorithmic subject matter. The nine capabilities (soft-vote readout, token-ladder / product-quantizer, drift/noise co-channels, inference-time fusion, guarded recalibration, label-free self-twin monitor, selective-fidelity and channel-attribution) are the program's filed and deposited methods, and the separability screen is previously published; k-means and vector quantization, Fisher discriminant analysis, nearest-centroid and k-nearest-neighbor classification, random forests, product quantization, a distance-based out-of-distribution detector, a two-sample shift detector, pretrained time-series foundation models used only as comparators, and principal-component analysis are established prior art or standard tools, used only as tools or comparators. The method characterized — the class-discriminant single-token codebook encoder, its composable capabilities, and its label-free nearest-centroid novelty score (the filed self-twin / Tier-0 gate), together with the previously published separability screen — is the subject of filed and pending U.S. patent applications held by the authors, or is already published. The per-deployment configuration-selection and input-conditioning procedure, and the silicon productization and commissioning toolchain, are retained as trade secrets and deliberately not disclosed; the platform is characterized here with the plain labeled capabilities, the published screen, and the measured envelope. title: Protecting Privacy through a Responsible Decryption Policy
abstract: TABLE OF CONTENTS I. INTRODUCTION II. ENCRYPTION III. DOCUMENT PROTECTION AND THE ACT OF PRODUCTION DOCTRINE A. The Doctrine Today B. Encryption Does Not Fit Neatly into the Act of Production Doctrine C. The Future of Encryption Analyzed Under Document Production: Government Hover Orders IV. FINDING THE FIFTH AMENDMENT BALANCE A. Balancing the Purposes and Practical Realities of the Fifth Amendment Privilege B. A Responsible Decryption Policy V. CONCLUSION I. INTRODUCTION In late December 2006, Sebastien Boucher crossed into Vermont from Canada. (1) At the border, customs officials inspected Boucher's car and found a laptop in the back seat. (2) A customs agent accessed the computer without entering a password and initiated a search for media files; the query returned tens of of images. (3) Later, a special agent continuing the investigation found thousands of images of adult pornography and animation depicting adult and child pornography. (4) At this point, Boucher was detained, read his Miranda rights, and questioned by the agents. (5) At their request, Boucher showed the investigators where his downloaded files were located on the laptop. (6) The agents did not see Boucher enter any password in order to access the files, which were maintained on a hard drive designated as drive. (7) After the agents found several pornographic images and videos of children, they seized the laptop and arrested Boucher. (8) Several days later, officers accessed the laptop and created a mirror image of the hard drive, yet they were unable to access drive Z because it was protected by an encryption algorithm. (9) An agent versed in computer forensics examined the drive and later testified that it would be virtually impossible to access the files, (10) as it would take years to unlock the drive without a password. (11) The grand jury subpoenaed Boucher, demanding that he provide all documents, whether in electronic or paper form, reflecting any passwords used or associated with the [computer in question]. (12) Boucher resisted the subpoena, stating that it violated his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. (13) Initially, Magistrate Judge Niedermeier found that forcing Boucher to disclose the password would effectively compel him to testify against himself (14) and quashed the subpoena. (15) Although Chief Judge Sessions later overturned that decision, (16) the original order would have left law enforcement agents unable to catalogue or present as evidence the illegal pornography they knew Boucher possessed. (17) Boucher is hardly the first time the government has grappled with the seemingly modern issue of data encryption. In 1776, then General George Washington discovered his Chief of Hospitals was sending coded letters to the British concerning the colonial army's supply levels and troop movements. (18) During Aaron Burr's trial for treason in the early 1800s, prosecutors requested that his secretary decipher Burr's personal correspondence, only to have the secretary refuse on Fifth Amendment grounds. (19) However, in each of these cases the government was able to recover the sought-after information simply by breaking the encryption code. (20) Today, the widespread availability of powerful encryption software guarantees that law enforcement will increasingly confront this problem without the ability to break the code in a reasonable amount of time. Although Chief Judge Sessions permitted law enforcement access to the encrypted files, his ruling depended largely on the fact that Boucher had already voluntarily provided agents with access. (21) Absent this fact, law enforcement would be left facing practically unbreakable encryption with no reasonable recourse to secure important evidence. (22) This Note argues that the magistrate judge's analysis in Boucher I mischaracterizes the encryption issue. …
